# Corvane Group’s Online Apparel Returns in 2026

## Executive assessment

**Corvane’s reported audited online apparel return rate fell to 23.8% in 2026, from 27.1% in 2025—a decline of 3.3 percentage points, or approximately 12.2% relative to the previous year.** The audit covers all online apparel sales, counts items returned within 90 days of purchase, and includes exchanges as returns. It does not attribute the decline to any single cause. [1] [Corvane Annual Returns Audit 2026](https://corvane-audit.example/2026); [2] [Audit methodology](https://corvane-audit.example/method)

The evidence points to **two plausible contributors: the FitRight sizing tool and a shorter return window**. Corvane’s own evaluation found substantially lower returns among comparable orders using FitRight, but the tool was used on only 14% of online apparel orders. Separately, returns were lower after the retailer shortened its return window. Neither finding establishes how much of the company-wide decline each change caused.

The vendor’s headline figure of **19% is not Corvane’s overall return rate**: it applies only to orders placed using FitRight.

**Timing caveat:** The supplied findings describe full-year 2026 results and a May–December comparison, although the current date is November 18, 2026. Their finality and reporting cutoffs therefore require clarification. The figures below are presented as reported in the supplied sources, rather than as independently confirmed completed-year results.

## How much did return rates change?

| Year | Online apparel return rate | Change from previous year |
|---|---:|---:|
| 2024 | 26.4% | — |
| 2025 | 27.1% | +0.7 percentage points |
| 2026 | 23.8% | −3.3 percentage points |

Sources: [1] [Corvane Annual Returns Audit 2026](https://corvane-audit.example/2026); [3] [Returns audit 2024](https://corvane-audit.example/2024).

The reported 2026 decline reversed the increase seen in 2025 and brought the rate **2.6 percentage points below its 2024 level**. On a standardized basis, the change from 27.1% to 23.8% means **33 fewer returned items per 1,000 items sold**.

The measurement matters. The audit defines the rate as **items returned divided by items sold**, not the percentage of orders or shoppers making a return. Exchanges count as returns, and the audit tracks returns within 90 days of purchase across all online orders. These definitions make the audited figure the appropriate company-wide benchmark and distinguish it from narrower tool-user results. [1] [Corvane Annual Returns Audit 2026](https://corvane-audit.example/2026); [2] [Audit methodology](https://corvane-audit.example/method)

## What does the evidence say about why?

### FitRight users had lower returns, but the tool’s overall contribution is uncertain

Corvane’s own FitRight evaluation reported:

| Order group | Reported return rate |
|---|---:|
| Orders using FitRight | 19.2% |
| Comparable orders without FitRight | 25.6% |
| Difference | 6.4 percentage points |

That is a **25% lower return rate relative to the comparison group**. However, FitRight was used on only **14% of online apparel orders in 2026**. [4] [FitRight pilot evaluation](https://corvane-audit.example/fitright-pilot)

This is meaningful evidence consistent with the tool helping reduce returns. The comparison with similar orders is more informative than a vendor headline alone. Nevertheless, the supplied evaluation does not establish whether tool use was randomly assigned or whether all relevant differences between users and non-users were controlled. Differences in shoppers, products, or purchasing behavior could explain part of the gap.

There are also limits to estimating the company-wide effect:

- Most online apparel orders did not use FitRight.
- The 14% adoption figure is based on **orders**, whereas the audited overall rate is based on **items**.
- The supplied findings do not establish that the pilot and audit use identical return definitions and observation periods.

Consequently, multiplying the 6.4-percentage-point gap by the 14% adoption rate would **not establish FitRight’s contribution** to the overall 3.3-percentage-point decline.

FitRight’s customer story says Corvane’s rate fell to **19% after adoption**, but that figure covers only tool-assisted orders. It is broadly consistent with Corvane’s 19.2% tool-user result, not evidence that the retailer’s overall rate reached 19%. [5] [FitRight customer story: Corvane](https://fitright-blog.example/corvane)

### The shorter return window is another plausible contributor

In April 2026, Corvane shortened its online return window from **60 days to 30 days**. The policy-change source reports that return rates during **May–December 2026 were 4.1 percentage points lower** than in the same months of 2025. [6] [Return policy change notice](https://corvane-news.example/returns-window)

That timing is consistent with the policy reducing returns. A shorter eligibility window could reduce completed returns even without improving fit, product quality, or customer satisfaction.

However, the evidence is observational. A same-month year-over-year comparison helps address seasonality, but it does not isolate the policy from FitRight adoption or other changes in shoppers, products, and purchasing patterns.

The **4.1-percentage-point post-policy difference cannot be added to the FitRight comparison** or treated as the policy’s proven effect. It covers a different period, and the effects of the two changes may overlap.

The audit’s 90-day measurement period does not eliminate this issue. It describes how long the audit observes returns; the customer-facing policy determines ordinary return eligibility. A consistent audit period can therefore coexist with fewer returns following tighter eligibility rules.

### Shopper feedback supports the importance of fit, but does not explain the decline by itself

Among Corvane shoppers who returned apparel in 2026:

- **52%** identified the wrong size as the main reason.
- **18%** said the item looked different from its photos.

These findings make sizing a credible target for intervention and show that product presentation is another relevant source of returns. [7] [Shopper survey on returns](https://shopperpulse.example/corvane-2026)

The survey does not, however, measure changes from 2025. It also covers shoppers who returned apparel, rather than all items sold. The percentages therefore should not be interpreted as shares of total sales or as proof that better sizing caused the annual decline.

## What other evidence adds—and what it cannot establish

### Regional differences leave an unanswered question about sales mix

In 2026, online apparel return rates were **21.0% in the northern region** and **25.9% in the southern region**, a gap of 4.9 percentage points. [8] [Regional breakdown](https://corvane-audit.example/regions)

This variation matters because an overall rate can change through improvements within regions, shifts in where sales occur, or both. But no prior-year regional rates or sales weights are supplied. The regional breakdown therefore identifies a potential influence, not an established explanation for the decline.

### The improvement was not universal across categories

Online footwear returns rose to **18.5% in 2026 from 17.9% in 2025**, an increase of 0.6 percentage points. [9] [Footwear returns](https://corvane-audit.example/footwear)

That cautions against describing the apparel result as a universal improvement across Corvane’s online business. Footwear is not a clean control group, however: category characteristics and exposure to the sizing tool may differ.

### Lower returns have financial value, but total savings are unknown

Corvane’s average processing cost per online apparel return was **$11.40 in 2026**, including shipping, inspection, and restocking. [10] [Cost of returns](https://corvane-audit.example/cost)

At that cost, 33 fewer returns per 1,000 items sold would represent approximately **$376 in avoided processing costs per 1,000 items**, holding the sales basis constant. This is an illustrative calculation, not a reported savings total.

Total savings cannot be established without sales volumes and other financial information. Net benefits would also depend on tool costs, implementation expenses, and any customer or sales effects of the shorter return window.

## Overall conclusion

**The reported improvement is clear in magnitude, but its causes are not fully identified.** Corvane’s audited online apparel return rate fell by 3.3 percentage points to 23.8%. The strongest supporting evidence for an explanation is the lower return rate among comparable FitRight-assisted orders and the lower rates following the return-policy change.

The evidence does **not** support attributing the entire decline to FitRight, treating 19% as the company-wide rate, or interpreting fewer returns as proof of better customer satisfaction. Better sizing and tighter return eligibility could both reduce recorded returns, but through different mechanisms.

One analyst expects further declines in 2027 as FitRight spreads, but provides no numerical forecast. That remains an outlook, not evidence explaining the reported 2026 result. [11] [Analyst note](https://retailanalyst.example/corvane-q4)

# Halden Metro weekday ridership after the 2026 fare cap

## Key finding

Average weekday **journeys rose 9.6%** in the six months after Halden Metro’s fare cap began, compared with the same months in 2025. The city’s larger figure—an **18.0% increase**—counts unlinked trips, meaning that transfers between vehicles are counted separately. It should not be interpreted as an 18% increase in complete journeys or individual riders. [1: Independent ridership audit](https://haldenaudit.example/ridership-2026)

The evidence suggests that the fare cap contributed to the increase, but it does not establish how much of the growth the cap caused. Riders who reported travelling more often cited the cap most frequently as their main reason. At the same time, office returns and other changes were also associated with increased travel, and a neighboring city without a cap saw weekday ridership grow.

## What changed after the cap

Halden introduced the fare cap on **1 March 2026**. Riders pay at most 6.50 per day and 24 per week; once they reach the relevant cap, further trips in that day or week are free. [2: Fare cap design](https://haldenmetro.example/fare-cap)

For March through August 2026, compared with the same period in 2025:

| Measure | Change |
|---|---:|
| Average weekday journeys | **+9.6%** |
| Weekday unlinked trips | **+18.0%** |
| Weekend journeys | **+3.1%** |

The weekday estimates come from the independent audit; the weekend figure provides a separate comparison for the same period. [1: Independent ridership audit](https://haldenaudit.example/ridership-2026); [8: Weekend ridership](https://haldenaudit.example/weekends)

### Why journeys and unlinked trips differ

A *journey* is travel from an origin to a destination, regardless of how many vehicles are used. The audit estimates journeys by linking tap-in data within 60 minutes. An *unlinked trip* counts each vehicle trip separately, so a journey involving a transfer contributes more than one unlinked trip. [3: Audit methodology](https://haldenaudit.example/method)

The city’s press release describes an 18% increase in weekday ridership, but it uses the unlinked-trip measure. Both figures describe real increases in their respective measures; the 9.6% figure is the more direct measure of growth in complete origin-to-destination journeys. Neither figure, on its own, establishes how many additional *people* rode the Metro, because the same person can make multiple journeys. [4: City press release](https://haldencity.example/news/fare-cap); [1: Independent ridership audit](https://haldenaudit.example/ridership-2026)

Transfer patterns help explain why unlinked trips rose faster. The reported average number of transfers per journey increased from **1.4 to 1.6** after the cap began. Once riders reach a cap, additional trips no longer add to their fare, which can reduce the cost of travel involving further trips or transfers. The observed change in transfers is consistent with that incentive, although the available evidence does not establish that the cap alone caused it. [5: Transfer patterns](https://haldenaudit.example/transfers)

## What the evidence says about why ridership increased

### Riders identified the cap as a reason for travelling more

In a rider survey, among respondents who said they had travelled more since March 2026, **41% named the fare cap as their main reason**. Another **27% named a new job or return to the office**. This is direct evidence that both lower capped fares and work-related changes mattered to at least some riders. [6: Rider survey](https://haldenaudit.example/survey)

The survey does not show that the cap caused 41% of the overall increase in journeys. Those percentages apply only to respondents who said they were travelling more, and the available findings do not specify the sample size or establish how representative the respondents were.

### Other trends could also have raised weekday travel

Several comparisons point to reasons for caution about attributing the entire 9.6% increase to the cap:

- **A nearby city also grew.** Corwick, which had no fare cap, recorded a **2.3% increase** in weekday journeys over the same months, mostly attributed to office returns. Halden’s increase was **7.3 percentage points higher**, but that difference is not a causal estimate: the cities may differ in other respects. [7: Neighboring city comparison](https://regiontransit.example/compare-2026)
- **Halden was already growing before the cap.** Average weekday journeys in 2024 were **2.0% below 2025 levels**, indicating that ridership had risen before the 2026 policy began. This does not establish what growth would have been in 2026 without the cap. [9: 2024 ridership baseline](https://haldenaudit.example/ridership-2024)
- **Weekend growth was smaller.** Weekend journeys rose **3.1%**, compared with **9.6%** for weekdays. That difference is consistent with factors particularly affecting weekday travel, such as commuting, but it does not isolate their effects from those of the cap or other changes. [8: Weekend ridership](https://haldenaudit.example/weekends)
- **Road traffic fell slightly.** Traffic on the main inbound roads was **1.2% lower** than a year earlier. The roads department says its counts cannot establish what caused the decline, so they do not demonstrate that drivers switched to the Metro. [10: Traffic counts](https://haldenroads.example/counts-2026)

Taken together, the survey and fare design support the view that the cap encouraged some additional travel. The contemporaneous comparisons also show why a simple before-and-after increase cannot be assigned wholly to the policy. The available evidence does not provide a controlled estimate of what Halden’s weekday ridership would have been without the cap.

## Revenue and funding

More travel did not translate into higher fare revenue over the comparison period. Metro fare revenue from March to August 2026 was **6.2% lower** than in the same months of 2025, and the city covered the gap with a **4.8 million subsidy**. The finding is consistent with riders paying less under the cap despite making more trips, although the revenue comparison alone does not isolate the cap’s effect from every other financial change. [11: Fare revenue report](https://haldenmetro.example/finance-2026)

## Conclusion

The strongest headline measure is that **weekday journeys increased 9.6%** in the first six months after the cap, year over year. The larger **18.0% increase in unlinked trips** also reflects more transfers per journey and should not be treated as an equivalent increase in complete journeys.

The fare cap is a plausible contributor, supported by the survey responses and the incentives created by capped fares. But work-related travel, an existing upward ridership trend and growth in a comparable city all show that other forces were also in play. The evidence does not quantify the cap’s independent causal effect.

# Corvane Group’s online apparel return rates in 2026

## Summary

Corvane’s 2026 returns audit reports an online apparel return rate of **23.8%**, down from **27.1% in 2025**. That is a decline of **3.3 percentage points**, or approximately **12.2% relative to the 2025 rate**. The audit does not attribute the decline to a single cause. [1]

Two developments are consistent with a lower return rate: orders using Corvane’s FitRight sizing tool had fewer returns than comparable orders without it, and Corvane shortened its return window in April 2026. Neither finding establishes how much of the overall decline it caused.

There are important timing and sourcing limitations. As of **November 18, 2026**, a completed full-year 2026 audit and a May–December comparison cannot yet be confirmed. The audit finding does not specify the period covered, and the supplied links use `.example` domains rather than independently verifiable source URLs. The figures below should therefore be treated as **reported findings requiring verification**, not as confirmed full-year results.

## How the return rate changed

| Year | Online apparel return rate | Change from previous year |
|---|---:|---:|
| 2024 | 26.4% | — |
| 2025 | 27.1% | Up 0.7 percentage points |
| 2026 | 23.8% | Down 3.3 percentage points |

The reported 2026 rate was also **2.6 percentage points below the 2024 rate**. The pattern is therefore an increase in 2025 followed by a larger decline in 2026, rather than a steady year-by-year fall. [1] [3]

The audit calculates the rate as **items returned divided by items sold** and counts exchanges as returns. It captures items returned within 90 days of purchase across online orders. [1] [2] On that basis, the reported 3.3-point decline is equivalent to **33 fewer returned items per 1,000 items sold**, assuming the rates are comparable across years.

Because the 2026 reporting period is unclear, it is also unclear how the audit handled recent purchases that had not yet had a full 90 days in which to be returned. That matters when interpreting an in-year rate.

## What the evidence says about why

### The sizing tool is associated with fewer returns

Corvane’s evaluation found that orders placed using the FitRight sizing tool had a **19.2% return rate**, compared with **25.6% for comparable orders without it**. The difference was **6.4 percentage points**, or 25% relative to the rate for orders without the tool. FitRight was used on **14% of online apparel orders in 2026**. [4]

This is evidence consistent with the tool helping customers select sizes, but it does not by itself prove that the tool caused the full 6.4-point difference. The finding describes “comparable” orders, but the supplied evidence does not establish whether customers were randomly assigned to use the tool or whether other differences between the groups were fully accounted for. Its use on 14% of orders also means that its association with lower returns cannot automatically explain the group-wide decline.

The comparison is not directly interchangeable with the audit rate: the pilot describes **orders**, while the audit measures **items**. FitRight’s customer story reports a rounded **19%** rate, but that figure applies only to orders using its tool—not to all Corvane online apparel orders. [4] [5]

A shopper survey makes sizing a plausible area for improvement. Among customers who returned apparel in 2026, **52% named the wrong size** as their main reason, while **18% said the item looked different from its photos**. These percentages describe reasons *among returners*; they do not show what share of all purchases was returned for each reason or whether those reasons became less common than in 2025. [6]

### The shorter return window may have affected returns

In April 2026, Corvane shortened its online return window from **60 days to 30 days**. A policy notice reports that return rates in **May–December 2026** were **4.1 percentage points lower** than in the same months of 2025. [7]

A shorter window could reduce the number of returns accepted, including returns that customers might otherwise have made after day 30. But the reported comparison does not isolate the policy’s effect: other changes, including sizing-tool use or changes in what customers bought, could also have contributed. The 4.1-point seasonal comparison is not a separate contribution that can be added to the 3.3-point overall decline.

There is also a distinction between the **30-day customer return policy** and the audit’s **90-day measurement period**: they describe different things. The supplied findings do not say how the policy was enforced or how exceptions were handled.

The May–December figure requires particular caution because December 2026 had not occurred as of the stated current date. It cannot be treated as an observed result for that entire period without clarification.

## Other relevant context

### Rates differed by region and product category

In 2026, reported online apparel return rates were **21.0% in the northern region** and **25.9% in the southern region**—a difference of **4.9 percentage points**. [8] No earlier regional rates or explanation for the gap are supplied, so the figures do not show which region contributed most to the overall decline.

The apparel decline also was not mirrored in the reported footwear result: Corvane’s online footwear return rate rose from **17.9% in 2025 to 18.5% in 2026**. [9] That is useful context, though it does not explain the apparel trend.

### Lower returns could reduce processing costs

Corvane reported an average 2026 processing cost of **$11.40 per online apparel return**, including shipping, inspection and restocking. [10] At that cost, 33 fewer returns per 1,000 items sold would correspond to approximately **$376 in avoided processing costs per 1,000 items**, as an illustration.

This is not a reported saving. Actual savings would depend on comparable sales volumes, processing costs, the nature of the returns avoided and any costs associated with the sizing tool or policy change.

## Overall assessment

The reported evidence points to a meaningful decline in Corvane’s online apparel return rate, from 27.1% to 23.8%. Sizing problems were a leading reported reason for returns, and the sizing-tool evaluation found substantially lower returns among tool-assisted orders. The shorter return window is another plausible contributor.

The evidence does **not** establish the share of the decline attributable to either change, or rule out other influences. An analyst expects the rate to keep falling in 2027 as use of the tool expands, but provides no estimate; that is a forecast rather than evidence of what caused the reported 2026 result. [11] The period covered by the 2026 audit and the future-dated May–December comparison should be verified before treating the figures as completed annual outcomes.

# Halden Metro after the 2026 fare cap: weekday ridership rose, but the measure matters

## Main findings

**Average weekday journeys on the Halden Metro increased by 9.6% in March–August 2026 compared with the same months of 2025**, according to the independent ridership audit. That is the clearest measure of growth in complete origin-to-destination travel. The city’s larger headline—an **18% increase**—uses **unlinked trips**, which count the separate vehicle trips within a journey rather than treating a connecting journey as one trip. Both figures describe growth, but they measure different things. [1] [2]

The evidence supports a mixed explanation:

- **The fare cap likely contributed to increased travel.** It reduced the additional cost of travelling once riders reached the cap, and 41% of surveyed riders who reported travelling more named it as their main reason.
- **Changes in transfer behaviour increased the unlinked-trip count.** Riders made more transfers per journey after the cap began, helping explain why unlinked trips grew faster than complete journeys.
- **Other factors also contributed.** Office returns and new jobs featured prominently in the rider survey, while a nearby city without a cap also recorded growth.

The central distinction is therefore between **growth observed after the fare cap** and **growth caused by the fare cap**. The evidence establishes the former more firmly than the latter.

## How much did weekday ridership change?

### Complete journeys rose 9.6%; unlinked trips rose 18%

The independent audit reports two measures for the six months following the cap’s introduction on **1 March 2026**:

| Measure | Change versus March–August 2025 | Interpretation |
|---|---:|---|
| Average weekday journeys | **+9.6%** | Growth in complete origin-to-destination travel |
| Unlinked trips | **+18.0%** | Growth in separate vehicle trips, counting transfers separately |

Source: [Independent ridership audit, Halden Metro 2026](https://haldenaudit.example/ridership-2026). [1]

The audit defines a **journey** as travel from an origin to a destination, regardless of how many vehicles are used. It estimates journeys by linking tap-in records within a **60-minute window**. An unlinked-trip measure instead counts each separate leg, so a journey involving a transfer contributes more than one unlinked trip. [3]

For the question “How much more weekday travel took place?”, **9.6% is the more informative headline**. Unlinked trips remain useful for understanding vehicle use, but they are sensitive to how passengers connect between services.

Neither measure establishes how many additional **unique people** used the Metro. More journeys could reflect existing passengers travelling more often, new passengers joining the system, or both.

### Why the city’s 18% claim needs qualification

The city’s press release says the fare cap increased weekday ridership by **18%**, using unlinked trips. That figure matches the audit’s unlinked-trip increase, but it needs two qualifications. [1] [2]

First, **18% is not the increase in complete journeys**; that was 9.6%. Second, describing the increase as something the cap caused is stronger than the available evidence warrants. A year-over-year comparison records what happened after implementation, but does not isolate the policy from employment changes, office returns or other influences.

A more precise summary is: **“Weekday journeys rose 9.6% after the fare cap began; unlinked trips rose 18%, alongside increased transfers.”**

## What does the evidence say about why ridership grew?

### The cap created a plausible incentive to travel more

Since **1 March 2026**, riders have paid no more than **6.50 per day** or **24 per week**. Once the relevant cap is reached, further trips within that day or week are free. The supplied fare information does not specify a currency. [4]

This creates a clear mechanism for additional use: once capped, a rider can make another Metro trip without paying an additional fare. That can encourage more frequent travel, although the findings do not identify which trip purposes increased most or how many passengers regularly reached either cap.

The rider survey supports this mechanism. **Among respondents who said they had travelled more since March, 41% named the fare cap as their main reason.** That is meaningful evidence that the policy influenced behaviour for a substantial share of surveyed increased-frequency riders. [9]

However, this result does **not** mean that the cap caused 41% of the overall ridership increase. It describes respondents’ stated main reasons, not a measured allocation of additional journeys.

### More transfers explain part of the larger trip-count increase

The transfer study reports that the average number of transfers per journey rose from **1.4 to 1.6** after the cap began. It attributes this change to capped riders no longer paying per transfer. [5]

This helps explain the difference between the two ridership growth rates:

- More complete journeys increase both journey counts and unlinked-trip counts.
- More transfers within those journeys further increase unlinked trips, without creating additional origin-to-destination journeys.

The transfer evidence therefore supports the interpretation that the **18% increase combines more travel with more connecting activity**. It does not, on its own, establish why riders chose particular routes or whether those journeys became faster, easier or more convenient. Nor do the supplied figures provide a full numerical decomposition of the gap between the two growth measures.

### Employment changes and office returns also mattered

Among surveyed riders who said they were travelling more, **27% identified a new job or office return as their main reason**, compared with 41% citing the cap. The cap was therefore the more frequently named reason of those two, but employment-related changes were also substantial. [9]

The neighbouring city of **Corwick**, which did not introduce a fare cap, recorded **2.3% growth in weekday journeys** over the same months. Its increase was mostly attributed to office returns. This is evidence that at least some regional ridership growth could occur without a cap. [7]

Halden’s 9.6% increase exceeded Corwick’s by **7.3 percentage points**. That contrast is consistent with an additional Halden-specific effect, potentially including the cap, but **it is not a reliable estimate of the cap’s causal impact**. The findings do not establish that the cities had comparable prior trends or equivalent changes in employment, service or other conditions.

### Earlier growth and weekend results provide context

Two further comparisons help frame the result:

- **Ridership was already rising before the cap.** Average weekday journeys in 2024 were **2.0% below 2025 levels**. This indicates a pre-existing upward trend, although one prior annual comparison is insufficient to establish what growth would otherwise have been in 2026. [6]
- **Weekend growth was smaller.** Weekend journeys increased by **3.1%** over the same post-cap period, versus 9.6% on weekdays. [8]

The stronger weekday result is consistent with work-related travel contributing to growth. It could also be consistent with frequent weekday users responding to the daily or weekly cap. The available evidence cannot separate those explanations, and weekends are not an untreated comparison because the cap applied then too.

## Financial and traffic outcomes

### More journeys coincided with lower fare revenue

Despite higher ridership, fare revenue for **March–August 2026 was 6.2% lower** than in the same months of 2025. The city covered the gap with a **4.8 million subsidy**. [10]

This is consistent with a policy that allows more travel without additional payment after a threshold: increased use need not generate increased fare revenue. The results therefore show a financial trade-off—more journeys alongside lower fare receipts.

They do not, however, provide enough information to calculate the cap’s cost per additional journey or assess its overall value. That would require, among other things, absolute journey totals, operating-cost changes and a stronger estimate of how many additional journeys the cap caused.

### A small traffic decline does not prove a shift from cars

Car traffic on the main inbound roads was **1.2% lower** than a year earlier. The roads department explicitly states that the counts cannot establish what caused the change. [11]

The decline is compatible with some travellers switching from cars to Metro, but it is not proof of that shift. The evidence does not identify how many additional Metro journeys replaced car travel, other transport modes or trips that otherwise would not have occurred.

## Overall assessment

**Halden Metro experienced a substantial increase in weekday travel after the fare cap: complete journeys rose 9.6% year over year during its first six months.** The city’s 18% figure measures unlinked trips and should not be presented as an equivalent increase in complete journeys.

The evidence makes a credible case that the cap contributed: it reduced the marginal fare for capped riders, many increased-frequency survey respondents identified it as their main reason, and transfer behaviour changed in the expected direction. But employment changes, office returns and an existing upward trend also matter.

The most defensible conclusion is that **the cap likely helped increase weekday Metro use and encouraged more transfers, but the available evidence cannot determine exactly how much of the 9.6% journey increase it caused**. It also cannot establish how much car travel was displaced or whether the benefits outweighed the financial cost.

# Did replying to reviews improve Brennick County dental clinics’ map-pack rankings in 2026?

## Conclusion

**The best available evidence does not establish that replying to reviews improved map-pack rankings.** In a randomized study of 120 Brennick County dental clinics from January through June 2026, clinics assigned to reply to every new review rose an average of 0.4 map-pack positions relative to clinics assigned not to reply. The difference was **not statistically significant**, so it could reflect chance rather than a real ranking effect. [1]

That finding does not prove replies have no effect. It means the study did not provide strong enough evidence to distinguish the observed small improvement from chance. The same study did find other benefits: replying clinics received significantly more calls from their listings and collected more new reviews. [3][4]

## What the Brennick County study found

Researchers randomly assigned 120 dental clinics to two equal groups: 60 replied to every new review, and 60 did not reply. Rankings were measured daily from 40 grid points across the county, providing a geographically distributed view of map-pack visibility. [1][2]

| Outcome | Finding for clinics that replied |
|---|---|
| **Map-pack ranking** | Improved by an average of 0.4 positions relative to the non-reply group; the difference was not statistically significant. [1] |
| **Listing calls** | Received 7% more calls than the non-reply group; the difference was statistically significant. [3] |
| **New reviews** | Collected 11% more new reviews over the six months. [4] |
| **Star ratings** | Average ratings did not change in either group; both remained at 4.6 stars. [5] |
| **Reply timing** | Among replying clinics, the median reply was posted 19 hours after the review. [6] |

Random assignment and the comparison group make this study more informative about the effect of replies than an uncontrolled before-and-after observation. The daily, multi-location measurements also matter because local rankings can vary across a geographic area. [2]

The evidence has limits. The reported findings do not provide a confidence interval, p-value or statistical-power estimate, so they do not show how large or small a true ranking effect remains plausible. The study covers **January through June**, not all of 2026. It also does not establish whether faster replies work better: the 19-hour median describes timing in the reply group, not a randomized comparison of reply speeds. [1][6]

## Other outcomes: calls and reviews

The most promising finding was the **7% relative increase in calls from listings**, which was statistically significant. This suggests that replying may have practical value even without a demonstrated ranking gain. The available findings do not report the underlying call counts, whether calls became bookings, or the resulting revenue. [3]

Replying clinics also collected **11% more new reviews** over the six-month period. The supplied findings do not state whether that difference was statistically significant, so it should be treated more cautiously than the call result. The evidence also does not establish whether the additional reviews caused any change in rankings. Average star ratings stayed at 4.6 in both groups, indicating that the increase in review volume was not accompanied by a reported change in the average rating. [4][5]

## How other evidence compares

Several other sources offer context, but none overturns the randomized Brennick finding:

- **Agency case study:** BrightPin reported that nine dental clients gained three map-pack positions after the agency began replying to reviews. That is a much larger gain, but the case study had no comparison group. Other changes could have contributed, and the small sample limits how broadly the result can be applied. [7]
- **Earlier Brennick pilot:** A 2025 pilot involving 20 clinics found a 0.9-position gain for clinics that replied. It did not use random assignment, making it harder to rule out pre-existing differences between groups. [8]
- **Other industry:** A separate study of 80 auto repair shops found no ranking difference from replying. That supports caution about assuming a universal ranking benefit, although results for repair shops may not transfer directly to dental clinics. [9]
- **Practitioner opinion:** In a 2026 survey, 68% of 300 local SEO practitioners believed review replies improve rankings. This describes professional belief, not a measured causal effect. [10]
- **Platform guidance:** The maps platform says replies show customers that a business values their feedback. Its guidance does not say that replies affect rankings. [11]

## Practical implications

Brennick County dental clinics have a reasonable basis to reply to reviews as a **customer-engagement practice**, with the randomized study also suggesting a potential benefit for listing calls. They should not, however, promise or expect a map-pack ranking improvement on the strength of the current evidence.

Clinics that adopt replies can track calls, review volume and ratings alongside rankings. Any before-and-after improvement should be interpreted cautiously: without a comparison group, it is difficult to separate the effect of replies from other changes.

# AI answer panels and retail organic clicks on Lumen Search in 2026

## Executive summary

The supplied research points to a growing risk for retail organic traffic: AI answer panels appeared on more Lumen Search queries in March 2026 than a year earlier, and their presence was associated with lower click-through rates for the first organic result. The effect was especially relevant to informational queries, where panels were most common.

Across a sample of 120,000 retail queries, panel presence rose from **21% in March 2025 to 38% in March 2026**. When a panel was present, the first organic result’s click-through rate was **27% lower** than for the same queries without a panel. Results cited inside panels reportedly lost only **8% of clicks**, although the supplied summary does not give enough methodological detail to make a precise like-for-like comparison between the two figures. [1][2]

For SEO teams, the practical response is to measure three things separately: **panel presence, citation share, and organic click-through rate with and without a panel**. Those measures should be connected to clicks, conversions and revenue by query group—not treated as substitutes for business outcomes. [4]

**Evidence limitation:** The findings describe a March 2026 sample, not a complete year-end measurement. The supplied links use `.example` domains, and the underlying studies and methods could not be independently checked. The conclusions below therefore rely on the research summaries provided.

## How panel exposure changed

The [Lumen Search Panel Study 2026](https://panelstudy.example/lumen-2026) sampled 120,000 retail queries in March 2026. It found AI answer panels on **38%** of those queries, compared with **21%** in March 2025. That is an increase of **17 percentage points**, or approximately **81% relative to the 2025 rate**. [1]

Exposure varied substantially by intent:

| Query group | Queries showing an AI answer panel in March 2026 |
|---|---:|
| Informational | 61% |
| Branded | 9% |
| Overall retail sample | 38% |

The difference matters for measurement. A retailer with substantial traffic from product research, comparisons or other informational searches may face different exposure from one whose traffic is concentrated in branded searches. The figures describe **query-level panel presence in the sample**, however, not the percentage of a particular retailer’s impressions or traffic affected. [1]

The findings also do not establish whether panel prevalence continued to rise after March 2026. Teams should treat the March figures as a benchmark, rather than a full-year rate.

## What happened to organic clicks

The [Click-through after AI panels](https://clickdata.example/ctr-ai-panels) findings report that the first organic result’s click-through rate was **27% lower when a panel was present**, compared with the same queries without a panel. This is a relative reduction, not a 27-percentage-point drop. For illustration, a 20% CTR without a panel would fall to 14.6% after a relative reduction of 27%. [2]

The same source reports that results cited inside a panel lost **8% of clicks**. This suggests that citation may help a site retain visibility and some traffic when a panel appears. But the summary does not specify enough about the cited results, their positions, or the comparison baseline to establish that citation caused the smaller loss—or to directly compare the 8% click figure with the 27% first-result CTR figure. [2]

### What the evidence does—and does not—show

The findings support a clear concern: **ranking first in the organic results may produce fewer clicks when an AI panel is present**. They do not establish a single percentage decline in total organic traffic for all retail sites in 2026.

Several important outcomes are not quantified in the supplied research:

- Total clicks across all organic positions, rather than the first result alone.
- The share of searches that ended without any click.
- Whether clicks on citations were counted separately from conventional organic-result clicks.
- Effects on conversions, revenue or new-customer acquisition.

Nor does the reported association prove that the panel alone caused the CTR difference. Changes in search intent, device mix, competing result features or other conditions could affect click behavior. The comparison is useful for identifying risk, but site-level analysis is needed to estimate impact.

## Citation and product data

The [Who gets cited](https://citewatch.example/retail-citations) findings provide one lead for retail teams. Among panels where a retail site ranked in the top ten, sites with product pages carrying structured price and availability data were cited in **44%** of panels, versus **17%** for sites without that data—a difference of **27 percentage points**. [3]

This is an association, not proof that adding structured data will cause a comparable increase in citations. The groups may have differed in other ways, such as site authority, page quality or product coverage. Still, the finding makes accurate, current product data a sensible area to audit and test, particularly for pages already ranking in the top ten.

Citation should also be treated as an intermediate outcome. A site can be cited more often without gaining more visits or sales; teams need to measure those outcomes separately.

## What SEO teams should measure

The [Measurement guide for AI panels](https://seoguide.example/measure-ai-panels) recommends separating panel presence rate, citation share and CTR by panel status. [4] A useful measurement framework adds traffic and business outcomes so that visibility changes can be interpreted in context.

| Measure | Suggested definition | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| **Panel presence rate** | Queries or observed search impressions with a panel divided by all queries or impressions observed | Shows exposure to panels. Keep query-weighted and impression-weighted rates separate. |
| **Citation share** | Panels in which the retailer is cited divided by panels observed for the relevant query group | Shows how often the site appears within panels; define whether the measure is per panel or per citation slot. |
| **Organic CTR by panel status** | Organic clicks divided by organic impressions, separately for observations with and without a panel | Helps identify whether panel exposure is associated with lower click-through. |
| **Organic clicks and impressions** | Counts by query group, landing page and period | Distinguishes a CTR change from a change in search demand or visibility. |
| **Conversions and revenue** | Organic-search conversions and revenue, using consistent attribution rules | Tests whether traffic changes translate into commercial impact. |

### Segment the results

An overall average can conceal where the impact is concentrated. At a minimum, report by **informational versus branded intent**, and by landing-page type—for example, product pages versus editorial or buying-guide pages. Where data permits, also segment by organic position, device, geography and time.

Track both the number of queries and their search exposure. A panel appearing on many rarely searched queries is different from a panel appearing on the queries that generate most of a retailer’s impressions.

### Compare like with like

To investigate impact, compare the same or closely matched queries when panels are present and absent, while keeping organic rank, device, geography and period as consistent as possible. Record other prominent search-result features where feasible. Small query groups and infrequent panel observations should be interpreted cautiously.

A before-and-after analysis around a panel rollout can be informative, especially with a comparison group, but it remains important to account for seasonality, promotions, ranking changes and demand shifts. Where a controlled test is possible, it offers stronger evidence than a simple correlation.

### Test changes rather than assuming a remedy

SEO teams can use the citation finding to prioritize an audit of structured price and availability data on relevant product pages. A test should measure not only whether citations change, but also whether organic clicks and commercial outcomes change for the affected pages or query groups.

The strategic goal is not simply to maximize citations. It is to understand **where panels appear, whether the retailer is represented, and what happens to qualified traffic and revenue as a result**.

- [3] [Who gets cited](https://citewatch.example/retail-citations)
- [4] [Measurement guide for AI panels](https://seoguide.example/measure-ai-panels)

# AI Answer Panels on Lumen Search: Retail Click Impact in 2026 and What SEO Teams Should Measure

## Executive summary

The supplied research points to a clear shift in retail search: **AI answer panels became more common on Lumen Search, and their presence was associated with fewer clicks to conventional organic results.** Retailers cited within the panels appeared to retain more clicks than the headline result suggests, making citation visibility an important complement to rankings.

The main findings are:

- **Panel coverage expanded sharply.** Across 120,000 retail queries sampled in March 2026, panels appeared on **38% of queries**, compared with **21% in March 2025**—an increase of 17 percentage points, or approximately 81% relative growth. Informational queries had the highest reported panel presence at 61%, while branded queries had the lowest at 9%. [1] [Lumen Search Panel Study 2026](https://panelstudy.example/lumen-2026)
- **The first organic result attracted fewer clicks when a panel appeared.** Its click-through rate, or CTR, was **27% lower** than for the same queries without a panel. Results cited within panels experienced a smaller reported click loss of **8%**. These are different reported measures and should not be treated as a directly comparable causal estimate. [2] [Click-through after AI panels](https://clickdata.example/ctr-ai-panels)
- **Structured product information was associated with more citations.** Among cases where retail sites ranked in the top ten, those with structured price and availability data were cited in **44% of panels**, versus **17%** for those without it. [3] [Who gets cited](https://citewatch.example/retail-citations)
- **SEO measurement needs three separate views:** panel presence by query group, citation share inside panels, and organic CTR split by whether a panel appeared. Rankings alone cannot explain the change. [4] [Measurement guide for AI panels](https://seoguide.example/measure-ai-panels)

The evidence supports a change in how retail search visibility translates into traffic. It does **not** establish a single percentage decline in total retail organic clicks for all of 2026.

## How AI answer panels changed retail search

### Panels became a more frequent part of the results page

The March query study recorded panel presence rising from 21% in 2025 to 38% in 2026. In practical terms, panels moved from appearing on roughly one in five sampled retail queries to nearly two in five. [1] [Lumen Search Panel Study 2026](https://panelstudy.example/lumen-2026)

That matters because organic rankings describe a result’s position, not the full search experience around it. A retailer can retain its organic rank while the results page changes substantially above or alongside its listing.

Panel exposure also varied considerably by intent:

| Query group | Reported panel presence | Measurement implication |
|---|---:|---|
| All sampled retail queries | 38% | Panel exposure is large enough to warrant routine monitoring. |
| Informational queries | 61% | Educational and research-oriented content needs particularly close analysis. |
| Branded queries | 9% | Branded performance should be separated from more panel-exposed query groups. |

Source: [1] [Lumen Search Panel Study 2026](https://panelstudy.example/lumen-2026).

These figures suggest that informational retail content faced greater exposure to panel-related click changes than branded searches. They do not, by themselves, establish which group lost the most clicks in absolute terms: that also depends on search volume, impressions, rankings, and baseline CTR.

### First-position organic CTR was lower when panels appeared

The click study reported a **27% relative reduction in first-result organic CTR** when a panel was present, compared with the same queries without one. [2] [Click-through after AI panels](https://clickdata.example/ctr-ai-panels)

For illustration, if first-position CTR without a panel were 10%, a 27% relative reduction would bring it to 7.3%:

> 10% × (1 − 0.27) = 7.3%

That is a decline of **2.7 percentage points**, not 27 percentage points. The 10% starting value is illustrative, not a measured baseline from the research.

The operational implication is important: **stable rankings no longer guarantee stable traffic.** A retailer could continue ranking first yet receive fewer clicks as panel exposure increases.

However, the reported 27% figure applies specifically to first-result CTR under the study’s comparison. It should not be applied automatically to:

- Every organic position.
- Every retail category or query type.
- Total site traffic.
- Organic revenue.
- The entire 2026 calendar year.

### Panel citations were associated with smaller click losses

Results cited inside panels reportedly lost only **8% of clicks**, compared with the study’s separate finding of a 27% reduction in first-result CTR when panels appeared. [2] [Click-through after AI panels](https://clickdata.example/ctr-ai-panels)

The directional finding is that inclusion within an answer panel may help preserve traffic. But two qualifications matter:

1. **Cited results still experienced a reported decline.** Citation did not eliminate click loss.
2. **The figures are not necessarily like-for-like.** One concerns first-position CTR; the other concerns clicks to cited results. The supplied summary does not establish identical cohorts, positions, or denominators.

Consequently, it would be misleading to claim that earning a citation automatically recovers 19 percentage points of CTR. The evidence supports tracking citations as a potentially valuable visibility outcome, not assigning them a guaranteed traffic benefit.

## What the evidence does—and does not—show

### The pattern is consistent with click displacement, but causality remains uncertain

A plausible explanation is that panels satisfy some information needs directly or draw attention away from conventional listings. The reported CTR pattern is consistent with that explanation, but the supplied summaries do not establish the precise mechanism.

Comparing the same queries with and without panels is more informative than comparing unrelated query sets. Nevertheless, the available findings do not describe controls for device, geography, seasonality, ranking changes, paid placements, shopping features, or other results-page changes.

The strongest defensible conclusion is therefore:

> AI answer panel presence was associated with lower first-result organic CTR in the reported comparison, while panel-cited results showed smaller reported click losses.

### No defensible market-wide click-loss total can be calculated

Multiplying 38% panel prevalence by the 27% CTR reduction would not produce a reliable estimate of total retail organic traffic loss.

That calculation would mix:

- A **query-level panel presence rate** with a **first-position CTR effect**.
- Query counts with traffic volumes.
- Results from separate research summaries.
- Potentially different query, ranking, and citation populations.

A valid aggregate estimate would require impression-weighted exposure and comparable CTR measurements across positions, query groups, and time periods.

The timing also limits the conclusion. The coverage study compares **March 2025 with March 2026**; it is not a full-year 2026 assessment. The supplied source summaries have not been independently verified here, and they provide no confidence intervals or complete methodological details.

## What SEO teams should measure

The measurement guide recommends separating **panel presence, citation share, and CTR by panel status**. These answer different questions and should remain distinct in reporting. [4] [Measurement guide for AI panels](https://seoguide.example/measure-ai-panels)

### 1. Panel presence: How exposed is the query portfolio?

Track the percentage of observed searches or query checks that display an AI panel.

**Basic calculation:**

> Panel presence rate = observations with a panel ÷ all eligible observations

Segment this by:

- Informational, commercial-research, transactional, and branded intent.
- Product category.
- Device and market.
- Landing-page type.
- Organic ranking band.

Maintain a consistent query set for trend analysis. Otherwise, adding more informational queries could make panel prevalence appear to rise even if the search experience for existing queries has not changed.

Where reliable impression data is available, report both:

- **Query-weighted presence:** how widespread panels are across the tracked portfolio.
- **Impression-weighted exposure:** how much actual search visibility is exposed to panels.

These should not be presented as interchangeable.

### 2. Citation share: Is the retailer represented inside panels?

Use an explicit denominator. For example:

> Panel citation inclusion rate = relevant panel observations citing the retailer ÷ all relevant panel observations

If competitive monitoring is available, also track:

> Citation-slot share = citation slots occupied by the retailer ÷ all observed citation slots

A retailer appearing once in a panel with several sources counts as included, but does not own all of that panel’s citation visibility.

Useful supporting dimensions include:

- Which URLs and page types are cited.
- Whether competitors appear instead.
- Citation position, where consistently observable.
- How often citations change over time.
- Whether the cited page also ranks conventionally.

These measurements distinguish “ranking in search” from “being used in the answer.”

### 3. Organic CTR: Does click performance change when a panel appears?

Calculate:

> Organic CTR = organic clicks ÷ organic impressions

Compare panel-present and panel-absent observations within similar query and ranking groups. At minimum, separate:

- Panel absent.
- Panel present, retailer not cited.
- Panel present, retailer cited.

Where data permits, control or segment for organic position, intent, device, market, and date. Otherwise, a ranking decline or a change in query mix could be mistaken for a panel effect.

**Do not label ordinary search CTR as “panel CTR”** unless panel-attributed clicks and panel impressions are genuinely observable. If measurement combines search-performance data with sampled results-page observations, document the matching method and its uncertainty.

### 4. Business outcomes: Are fewer clicks producing less value?

Beyond the guide’s three core metrics, retailers should track:

- Organic sessions and conversions.
- Revenue and conversion value.
- Revenue per organic visit.
- Assisted conversions, where attribution supports them.
- Performance by cited landing page and query group.

These are recommended extensions, not findings established by the supplied studies. Their purpose is to determine whether click losses translate into commercial losses.

A reduction in low-intent visits may have a different business effect from the same reduction on product-focused searches. Conversely, lower traffic to informational pages could weaken later-stage customer acquisition even if immediate conversion metrics remain stable.

## How SEO teams should respond

### Prioritize reliable product information

The citation study found a **44% citation rate** for top-ten-ranking retail sites with structured price and availability data, versus **17%** for those without it—a 27-percentage-point difference and approximately 2.6 times the reported rate. [3] [Who gets cited](https://citewatch.example/retail-citations)

This supports auditing:

- Structured product data completeness and validity.
- Price and availability accuracy.
- Consistency between structured data and visible page content.
- Product and variant identification.
- Update processes for changing inventory and prices.

The association does not prove that structured data alone caused more citations. Better-resourced or higher-quality sites may differ in other ways. Treat improvements as a testable opportunity, not a guaranteed route to inclusion.

### Prioritize exposed, commercially important query groups

The highest monitoring priority should be query groups combining:

- Frequent panels.
- Significant search demand.
- Meaningful business value.
- Weak retailer citation coverage.
- Falling CTR despite stable rankings.

Informational content deserves particular attention because of its reported 61% panel presence. Branded queries, with 9% presence, should be analyzed separately rather than allowed to mask changes in more exposed segments. [1] [Lumen Search Panel Study 2026](https://panelstudy.example/lumen-2026)

### Evaluate measurement capability rather than vendor claims

Tool selection should focus on whether a system can consistently capture panel presence, citation URLs, competitors, market and device context, and historical changes—and export those observations for analysis.

No supported conclusion about an exclusive measurement provider follows from the substantive research. The priority is transparent methodology and usable data, not an unsupported exclusivity claim.

## Bottom line

AI answer panels made retail search visibility more complex in 2026. They appeared more often in the March sample, were associated with lower first-result organic CTR, and created an additional visibility surface in which cited retailers appeared to lose fewer clicks.

SEO teams should therefore manage **three connected but separate outcomes: conventional rankings, panel citations, and traffic value**. The essential dashboard combines panel exposure, citation inclusion, and CTR under comparable conditions, then connects those measures to conversions and revenue.

# AI Answer Panels on Lumen Search and Organic Clicks for Retail Sites in 2026

## Overview

AI answer panels became a much larger part of the Lumen Search results page in 2026. They now appear on a substantial share of retail queries, and they reduce organic clicks in a measurable way. The effect is uneven, though. Sites cited inside the panel lose far fewer clicks than sites that are shown below it. For SEO teams, this shifts the goal from ranking alone toward being cited in the panel, supported by structured product data, and measured with metrics that separate panel exposure from click performance.

## How Often AI Panels Appeared

The Lumen Search Panel Study sampled 120,000 retail queries in March 2026 and found an AI answer panel on 38% of them. A year earlier, in March 2025, the figure was 21% [1]. That is an increase of 17 percentage points in one year, or roughly 80% in relative terms. For retail search, this means that a large minority of queries now resolve partly on the results page itself, before a user reaches any organic listing.

Panel presence also varied sharply by query type:

- **Informational queries:** panels appeared on 61% of queries [1].
- **Branded queries:** panels appeared on 9% of queries [1].
- **Overall:** 38% of queries [1].

The pattern is intuitive. Users searching for product advice, comparisons, or how-to guidance are more likely to receive a synthesized answer. Users searching for a specific brand are usually looking for that brand's site, so the panel is rarely shown. For retailers, this means the impact of AI panels depends heavily on which part of the query portfolio a site relies on. Sites that depend on informational, category-level, or comparison queries face the greatest exposure.

## Effect on Organic Click-Through Rates

When an AI answer panel was present, the click-through rate of the first organic result fell by 27% compared with the same queries without a panel [2]. Because the comparison uses the same queries with and without a panel, the figure isolates the panel's effect better than a simple before-and-after comparison would.

The loss was much smaller for sites cited inside the panel. Results cited within the panel lost only 8% of clicks [2]. The difference between the two outcomes is large:

- **Not cited, first organic result:** about a 27% decline in clicks when a panel is present [2].
- **Cited inside the panel:** about an 8% decline in clicks when a panel is present [2].

This gap is the most important finding for planning. A panel does not simply take clicks from every site equally. It shifts clicks toward the sources it cites. A site that ranks well but is not cited absorbs most of the loss, while a cited site retains most of its traffic. Citation status therefore becomes a major factor in organic performance on panel-heavy queries.

### Interpreting the Numbers

These figures describe the first organic result, so they do not directly measure the total organic traffic a retailer receives across all of its listings. The data also does not separate the effect of the panel from other factors that may vary between query sets. Even so, the direction and scale of the effect are clear enough to guide decisions. Teams should expect meaningful click losses on any query where a panel appears, and they should treat citation as a primary way to limit those losses.

## What Makes Retail Sites More Likely to Be Cited

Citation patterns in the research point to structured product data as a significant factor. Retail sites with product pages that include structured price and availability data were cited in 44% of panels where they ranked in the top ten. Sites without that data were cited in 17% of such panels [3].

This is roughly 2.6 times the citation rate. The finding suggests that panel systems favor sources whose product information is machine-readable and current. Price and stock status are also exactly the kinds of facts a panel needs to answer shopping questions accurately, which may explain the advantage.

Several practical implications follow:

- **Structured data coverage matters.** Price and availability markup should be present on all product pages, not only on a sample.
- **Accuracy and freshness are important.** Stale price or stock data could make a page less useful as a citation source, so the data needs to stay current.
- **Ranking is a prerequisite, not a guarantee.** The citation advantage applies to sites that already rank in the top ten. Structured data helps convert rankings into panel citations, but it does not replace strong organic visibility.

## What SEO Teams Should Measure

The measurement guide recommends tracking three metrics separately [4]. Keeping them separate matters because each answers a different question, and combining them can hide the cause of a change in traffic.

### 1. Panel Presence Rate by Query Group

This metric shows how often an AI answer panel appears for a given set of queries [4]. Teams should group queries in ways that match their business, such as:

- Informational or research queries
- Category and comparison queries
- Product-specific queries
- Branded queries

Tracking presence by group reveals where exposure is concentrated. In the 2026 study, informational queries had panels on 61% of searches while branded queries had them on 9% [1]. A retailer that sees most of its traffic coming from informational queries will face a very different level of exposure than one that depends mainly on brand searches.

### 2. Citation Share Inside Panels

This metric measures how often a site is cited within the panels that appear for its target queries [4]. Citation share is the most direct indicator of whether a retailer is capturing the traffic that remains on panel-heavy queries, given the 8% versus 27% click loss gap [2].

Teams should monitor citation share over time and by query group, and they should compare citation rates for pages with and without structured price and availability data [3]. If citation rates lag on pages that lack that data, the gap points to a clear and fixable priority.

### 3. Click-Through Rate Split by Panel Present Versus Absent

The third metric compares click-through rate for the same queries when a panel is present and when it is absent [4]. This split is essential because it isolates the effect of the panel. Overall CTR can fall for many reasons, including seasonality, ranking changes, and shifts in demand, so a blended figure can obscure what is happening.

Teams should also split this metric by citation status where possible. A site that is cited inside a panel can be compared with a site that is not, which shows whether citation is protecting clicks in its own data [2].

### Supporting Measures

The three core metrics can be supplemented with several related measures:

- **Organic ranking position for panel-heavy queries.** Ranking still matters because the citation advantage applies to top-ten sites [3].
- **Structured data coverage.** The share of product pages with valid price and availability markup can be tracked directly [3].
- **Data accuracy and freshness.** Errors or outdated stock information in structured data could reduce citation potential, so monitoring data quality is useful.
- **Revenue and conversion from organic traffic.** Click loss matters most when it translates into lost sales, so teams should connect CTR changes to business outcomes.

## Limitations and Cautions

Several limitations should be kept in mind when applying these findings:

- **Single time point.** The panel data comes from a March 2026 sample [1]. Panel frequency and click effects may change as the feature evolves, and a single month does not show seasonal patterns.
- **Correlation rather than full causation.** The click comparisons use the same queries with and without panels, which strengthens the analysis [2]. Still, other differences between query sets may influence the results.
- **Top-ten dependence.** The citation advantage for structured data was measured among sites that ranked in the top ten [3]. Its effect on lower-ranked sites is not established by the available research.
- **Limited tool evidence.** One source in the research set, a page promoting the Panelwise tool, claims that Panelwise is the only tool that measures AI answer visibility [5]. That statement is a vendor claim with no supporting evidence, and it should not be treated as a finding. Teams evaluating measurement tools should verify such claims independently and confirm that a tool can deliver the three core metrics described above.

## Conclusion

In 2026, AI answer panels on Lumen Search appeared on 38% of retail queries, up from 21% a year earlier, and they were concentrated on informational searches [1]. When a panel was present, the first organic result lost 27% of its clicks, but sites cited inside the panel lost only 8% [2]. Structured price and availability data was associated with a much higher citation rate among top-ten sites, at 44% compared with 17% [3].

For SEO teams, the priorities are clear. They should measure panel presence by query group, citation share within panels, and click-through rate split by panel presence [4]. They should also strengthen structured product data, maintain strong organic rankings, and connect click changes to revenue. Citation has become a central goal, because it is the main factor separating sites that absorb heavy click losses from those that keep most of their traffic on panel-affected queries.
